summary: Proposes the Concise Data Definition Language, a notation for expressing CBOR data structures, and JSON structures as well. The goal is to describe protocol messages and data formats simply and unambiguously. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A short way to write down what shape some data must have, like a form with named blanks.

questions: what is concise data definition language
subtitle: A compact notation for describing exactly what shape a CBOR or JSON message must have.

tldr.problem: Protocols that use CBOR needed an easy, unambiguous way to say what a message or data item looks like, one that people can read and write and that machines can check.
tldr.mechanism: CDDL describes data with named rules built from types and groups. Arrays, maps, choices, occurrence markers, tags and control operators let a short text define the allowed structures.
tldr.outcome: CDDL is on the standards track and can also describe JSON, since the JSON data model is a subset of CBOR's. It is a notation for specifications and tools, not a code generator.

today: RFC 8610 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9682; it has not been obsoleted. The RFC itself says CDDL is meant for guiding human implementers, automated checking of CBOR and JSON data, and data analysis tools.

sections.title: Goals of CDDL
sections.content:
RFC 8610 defines the Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL), a notational convention for expressing Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) data structures. The main goal is a unified notation for protocols that use CBOR. The RFC lists six goals: an unambiguous description of the overall structure of a data item, flexibility in the ways data can be represented, the common CBOR datatypes and structures, one format that is both human-readable and machine-processable, automatic checking of data for compliance, and extraction of specific elements for further processing.

Using CDDL for JSON was not an original goal. It is a convenient side effect of the JSON data model being a subset of the CBOR data model.
sections.eli5: People who design data formats need a clear way to say what valid data looks like. CDDL is that way: short enough for people to read, strict enough for a computer to check against.

sections.title: Groups, Types and Choices
sections.content:
Maps and arrays can be used in four loosely distinct styles: a vector (an array of similar elements), a record (an array whose positions have different meanings), a table (a map with open keys and similar values) and a struct (a map whose keys are fixed by the specification). CDDL does not define these separately. It has one kind of composition, the group, and one other idea, the type.

A group is a list of entries, each a key and value pair. In an array only the values count and the names are documentation. In a map the names become keys, and order does not matter. A group can be given a name and reused, which avoids copy-and-paste between similar structures. The whole specification defines a type, and the first rule in the file is the root type. A group cannot be the root.

Types can be built as choices. A slash gives a type choice, as in protocol = 6 / 17, and a double slash gives a group choice. Ranges are written .. (inclusive) and ... (excluding the upper bound), and a leading & turns a group of named values into a choice, which is useful for enumerations. A hash mark followed by a major type number, such as #6.55799(breakfast), refers to the CBOR representation, for instance to use a tag.
sections.eli5: Everything is built from two blocks: a type, which says what kind of thing a value is, and a group, which is a list of named slots. You snap them together, and you can say a slot may be one of several kinds.

sections.title: Rules, Names and Occurrence
sections.content:
The basic syntax is inspired by ABNF. A rule is a name, an equals sign and a definition. Names are case sensitive, start with a letter and may contain hyphens, periods and a few other characters. Comments start with a semicolon and end at the end of the line. Text strings use double quotes, byte strings use single quotes and may be prefixed with h or b64, and hexadecimal numbers start with 0x. CDDL itself is encoded in UTF-8.

An occurrence indicator in front of an entry says how often it may appear: a question mark for optional, an asterisk for zero or more, a plus sign for one or more, or n*m with optional lower and upper limits. With no indicator, an entry occurs exactly once. CDDL can describe more flexibility than the target data model has: a map cannot repeat a key, so a repeated bedroom: size entry in a map effectively becomes optional.

CDDL predefines names for the primitive types, such as uint, nint, int, bool, float16, float32, float64, bstr or bytes, and tstr or text. A prelude of standard definitions is automatically prepended to every specification. CDDL leaves definite or indefinite-length encoding to the encoder.
sections.eli5: The notation is like writing a recipe card. Each line says what a thing is called and what it is made of, and little marks like a question mark mean this part is optional or can repeat.

sections.title: Arrays and Maps
sections.content:
An array is a group in square brackets, and a map is a group in curly braces. With [* person] the group person, a name and an age, repeats, giving values like ["aluminize", 212, "climograph", 4124]. In a record-style array, the key names in entries are ignored when encoding.

In a struct, an identifier followed by a colon becomes a text string key, called a bareword. Other key types use a double arrow, as in { * equipment-type => equipment-tolerances }. An entry with no occurrence indicator is mandatory, and an entry marked ? is optional. To allow unspecified extra entries, a spec can add the entry { * tstr => any }. A table is a map whose key type allows many values, such as {* x => y}.

Maps have no fixed order, so matching is more subtle than for arrays. The RFC warns against writing groups where a general entry comes before a specific one so that the match is indeterminate, and notes that tools cannot detect such cases. It also defines the cut, written ^. Once a key matches an entry that carries a cut, later entries can no longer match that key. The colon form includes the cut, so ? optional-key: int, * tstr => any does not accept optional-key with a non-integer value.
sections.eli5: An array is a numbered list where position matters. A map is a set of labeled boxes where only the label matters. A cut says that once a label is claimed by one rule, no other rule can use it.

sections.title: Controls and Their Registry
sections.content:
A control attaches an extra condition to a type, written target .operator controller. For example, bstr .size 4 limits a byte string to 4 bytes, and applied to an unsigned integer uint .size 3 limits its range to 24 bits. .bits says which bit numbers may be set, and .regexp requires a text string to match an XML Schema Definition regular expression.

.cbor and .cborseq say a byte string carries encoded CBOR, or a sequence of CBOR items. .and and .within intersect two types, with .within expressing that the left side is meant to be a subset of the right. The comparison controls .lt, .le, .gt and .ge work on numbers, .eq and .ne work on other values too, and .default marks a default value that is not sent over the wire.

IANA created a "CDDL Control Operators" registry holding these 14 names. New names without an internal dot need Specification Required, and names with an internal dot need IETF Review. The reviewer is told that other standards bodies may want controls for their own binary syntaxes.
sections.eli5: Controls are like extra stickers on a blank on the form: this answer must be exactly four bytes long, this number must be zero or more, this text must look like an email address.

sections.title: Tags, Unwrapping, Sockets and Generics
sections.content:
A CBOR tag is written #6.nnn(type), where nnn is the tag number. The prelude defines biguint = #6.2(bstr), and a spec can add more, such as buuid = #6.37(bstr). The unwrap operator ~ strips one layer from a named map, array or tag type, exposing its group or inner type. This allows reuse similar to inheritance, for example including all the entries of one header in another.

For extension points, a leading $ names a type socket and a leading $$ a group socket. They start out empty, and tools do not complain if they are never defined. Later rules, possibly in other files, add "plugs" with /= or //=. By convention all plugs must be augmentations.

Generics add parameters in angle brackets, as in message<t, v> = {type: t, value: v}, and can be used for both types and groups. The RFC also gives an operator precedence table, from loosest (=, /=, //=) to tightest (& and ~), and advises writers to add parentheses liberally.
sections.eli5: A socket is an empty plug-in slot in the spec. Anyone can later add a new piece that fits it, even in a separate file, without rewriting the original.

sections.title: Using CDDL with JSON
sections.content:
Because the JSON data model is a subset of CBOR's, CDDL can describe JSON by leaving out byte strings, tags and simple values other than false, true and null. Appendix E, which is normative, gives a limited prelude for this.

There are fine points. JSON has one kind of number, so uint, nint and int only test whether the number is integral, and 10, 10.0 and 1e1 all match uint. Specifying float16, float32 or float64 only limits the values to those the format can express. Interoperable integers in JSON lie between minus 2 to the 53rd power plus 1 and 2 to the 53rd power minus 1, so applications that need I-JSON compatibility may define limited types such as ij-uint = 0..9007199254740991. NaN and the infinities cannot be expressed in JSON even if the CDDL data model allows them.
sections.eli5: The same form can describe plain text data too. You just avoid the fancy blanks that text data cannot hold, such as raw bytes.

sections.title: Security and Usage Notes
sections.content:
CDDL itself does not bring security issues, but specifications of protocols that use CBOR need their own security analysis, following RFC 3552. The RFC suggests asking where the language could cause confusion that enables attacks, and says the security of a system ought not to depend on the correctness of a CDDL specification or implementation without further defenses. It also says that the impact of extension points on security needs careful consideration.

Writers are encouraged to value clarity and transparency over elegance, since CDDL making complexity easier to handle does not make the complexity less bad. Section 4 lists three uses: a guide for human implementers, automated checking of CBOR and JSON data, and data analysis tools. How strictly an application enforces the description is left to its designers, and a CDDL tool is not intended to write implementation code.
sections.eli5: The form itself is harmless, but a program that trusts a form without double-checking can still be fooled. So keep forms simple and clear, and keep other safety checks in place.
